How the UK’s Most Precious Military Icons Are Made
recentItems.description:
From its home in Haworth, West Yorkshire, Wyedean Weaving has spent more than 60 years supplying military uniforms, ceremonial regalia and insignia to the UK Armed Forces.
 
In this video, we go inside the workshop to see the incredible craftsmanship required to create these sacred items. Regimental colours are far more than just fabric—they are a living legacy of a unit's history, successes, and those who have fallen in battle.
 
Companies like Wyedean demonstrate the value of British centuries-old craftsmanship, innovation and family-run enterprise spanning four generations, preserving traditions and creating skilled local jobs.

In this video:

0:16 The history of Wyedean Weaving.
0:39 Why regimental colors are the most precious items in a unit.

recentItems.title: The British Army Like You've Never Seen Before
recentItems.description:
Inside Exercise RHINO BIZZ | BATUS, Canada

British soldiers deploy to BATUS, Canada for Exercise RHINO BIZZ — the Army's largest live recce-strike experimentation to date. Around 350 personnel from 2 PARA Battlegroup and 16 Air Assault Brigade combine drones, AI-enabled targeting, and electronic warfare in a contested training environment.

This is fifth-generation land warfare being built now, not promised for the future. Soldiers work alongside five embedded industry mission partners, testing live equipment in the field: FPV drones, autonomous systems, and the CAIN digital network connecting sensors to shooters in real time.

Go behind the scenes with the operators, coders, planners, and decision-makers making it happen — including medics using drones to deliver blood supplies in austere environments, and paratroopers using e-bikes with uncrewed systems to strike fast and extract.

Human-led. Technology-enabled. This is what modern service looks like.

recentItems.title: Modern warfare requires decision making not in minutes, but seconds.
recentItems.description:
From real-time reconnaissance to extending communications, the Puma drone is helping British soldiers stay one step ahead.
 
Watch how drones and AI are enhancing battlefield awareness and supporting faster decisions during training in Canada.

recentItems.title: What happens if a soldier needs blood on the battlefield?
recentItems.description:
During a recent British Army training exercise in Canada, every soldier's blood type was logged and tracked in real time as part of a simulated casualty scenario. If blood had been needed, medics could locate the nearest compatible donor—and a drone could deliver it straight to the casualty.
 
It's one of the innovations being tested as British soldiers prepare for a battlefield shaped by drones, AI and electronic warfare.
